title: Forty-Two
passages:
The handset was where Wren had folded it, a gray rubber brick with a bar on the side that you squeezed to talk and let go to listen. Dey got his thumb over the bar. It took him two tries. The first squeeze gave the deck a half second of open channel and the hiss of the storm, and he let go without a word, the way a man does when he has been about to say something for fourteen hours and finds it has moved somewhere he can't reach.

Wren kept working the bag. Four squeezes to the breath, a pause, four more; the bag was a rubber football with a one-way valve, and she had been at it long enough that her forearm had gone to shaking wire.

"Say it," she said. "Nobody down here is keeping score anymore. Sol's rule. It's in the log and everything."

Dey's lips were the color of the inside of a shell. He keyed the bar.

"Kettle low gate, this is the Marrow." Three words, a stop, three more. "Dey Okafor. I can't breathe. I need the lung rig. I'm asking."

The answer came back before he had let go of the bar. Quill had been sitting on the channel with the berth book open on her knee and the stylus behind her ear, waiting, because waiting was the job.

"Logged at the bell plus ten," she said. "Your name went in the book when you signed and it stays in whether you walk off this deck or not. The book doesn't strike. That's the price and it's already paid."

"Say the rest," Dey said.

"The lavage is a pump and a hose and forty liters of warm water. It flushes what's in your chest out of your chest. It doesn't mend what's torn. I've run it eleven times. Four sat up. Seven didn't, and I logged those too. The rig is lashed on the mole barge at the east mole and she has to cast off, cross the eye, and winch it over your rail. Nine minutes if the ebb lets her and it won't. The channel's shut to you, Marrow. It isn't shut to me."

"Nine minutes," Sol said. She was standing at the rail with her hand on nothing in particular, which was where her hand went when she'd lost the thread of a sentence and didn't want anybody to see her find it again. "Nia. What have we got."

"Six on the deck clock," Nia said, without looking up from the paper log open on her knee. "Dey's got six."

"That's the worst bedside manner on this coast," Dey told the handset.

"It's the only kind I've got," Quill said, and the channel hissed.

Dey dragged the bar down one more time. "Tell your barge I said please. First time in my life. I want it written down somewhere."

"It's written down."

Bayo had come up out of the well with grease to the elbow. He stood with his head cocked east, the way he stood when he was reading water instead of looking at it. "That's her casting off the mole," he said. "Two cylinders, and she knocks on the upstroke. Listen—"

The engine east of them changed note. It came off the knock and went smooth, and the whole sound of it swung, the way a hull swings when the man at the wheel puts the tiller over and the bow starts to come around.

Bayo's face did something small and unhelpful.

"Mole barge turns to starboard to clear the mole head," he said. "That one's coming about to port." He squinted into the rain, where there was nothing to squint at, no lamp, no masthead, no deck light, just the black line of the chop and the tower standing in it. "And she's running dark. Nobody runs dark in the eye unless they don't want to be counted."

"Bayo, on the drum," Sol said. "Nia, put the light on her."

The deck light was a sealed beam the size of a dinner plate on a two-meter mast, and it drank forty amps, which was why nobody lit it in weather. Nia threw the switch and the rain came out of the dark in a white sheet. East of them a low working hull sat in it with her wheelhouse shuttered and no masthead, no deck lamp, nothing on her that wanted to be counted.

"Log it," Sol said. "Barge, dark, closing. Inside a hundred meters you hit the horn and you don't ask anybody first."

Then she got down on the mat, put her hands over Wren's, and took the bag.

"Off," she said. "Go get harnessed."

Wren's fingers didn't want to straighten. She got them open one at a time and stood shaking out her arm, and behind her Sol picked up the count in the same flat voice Wren had been using for the last hour. Four squeezes and a pause. Four and a pause.

"You squeeze that like you're milking rope," Dey said.

"I've milked worse," Sol said. "Say when it's too fast."

Wren's harness was on the winch housing where she'd dropped it. The spit can was not on the clip. The clip was still there, an empty aluminum D-ring with the paint worn off it, and she put a spare carabiner through it so nothing would swing and knock her hip all the way down. It helped more than she wanted it to.

Salas already had his webbing on. Fourteen months out of the count and he still checked every buckle twice, and then he checked hers, which she let him do because it was faster than arguing with him.

"Talk me through it," he said.

She crouched by the drum and drew on the wet deck plate with her finger. "Forty-two meters. Five atmospheres sitting on top of you, so everything costs five times what it costs up here." She lifted the pony off the rack, a stubby steel bottle the length of her forearm, the second chance a diver carries on his hip for when the first one quits. "Nine minutes on the bottle. That's a deck number, that's one man standing in the sun. At forty-two it's a hundred and three seconds. One of us. Not two."

"Free-spool down," Salas said. "Drum pays out better than forty a minute. Call it a minute."

"A minute. Haul's the problem." She looked up at the drum. "Loaded, thirty a minute if she's kind. Eighty-four seconds up. Minute down, eighty-four up, a hundred and forty-four."

"And we've got a hundred and three."

"We're forty-one seconds short."

Bayo had his hand on the lever and wasn't pulling it. "Battery's the same arithmetic," he said. "Six lead bricks under the housing. They hold and they hold and then they come off a cliff all at once. Under load she's good for one pull. Ninety seconds of drum, then she's an anchor."

"So nobody drops the can and comes back for it," Sol said from the mat.

"Nobody's taking the short end either," Wren said. "Forty-one seconds. Somebody breathes water for forty-one seconds."

"I'll take it," Salas said. "I've done worse on less."

"You did fourteen months in a pocket on less and it cost you a man's face." Wren clipped the pony to his hip, not hers. "Don't tell me about worse."

Dey's hand came off the blanket and found her ankle. The grip was terrible. "You're going down for a can," he said, "while I lie here doing my fish impression."

"Yes."

"Good. Write down that I asked."

Nia wrote it down. She wrote the depths and the seconds after it, in pencil, in the paper log, because paper doesn't care about batteries or tides, and Wren watched her do it and understood that if the drum went slack at ninety seconds there would be a page aboard the Marrow saying exactly how.

Sol looked up from the bag. "Bayo. Drum."

East of them the dark engine was close enough now to hear over the rain, and it did not slow.

Bayo dropped the lever into the free-spool notch and the drum turned backward with a noise like a coin rolling downstairs.

"Brake band's mine," he said. "I let it go, you fall forty-two meters and the water stops you. That's the good version. Call my knots."

The ascent line was steel cable with an orange whipping every ten meters and a comms pair laid into the lay of it, two copper wires in a yellow sleeve, which was how a diver's mask talked to the deck and the deck talked back. Bayo kept his left thumb on the talk bar and his right palm flat on the band and let the cable run out through his glove.

"Your knots," Wren said. "I'll call your knots."

"Call them anyway."

Ten. The rail went up past her shoulders, then her helmet, then it was a gray line with a lamp on it, and then it was nothing at all. Green water, then bottle glass, then the color inside a bruise. Salas came down beside her feet first with one hand on the cable, the way he did everything.

Nia's voice came down the wire, flat as a ruler. "Nia to the drum. My brother asked me last night who owns who. He said *you own mine*. I went and checked the cold-box instead of answering him. The cold-box was fine. He's still waiting."

"Say the rest," Wren said.

"It's said. Nia owns Teo's, Teo owns Nia's, and it's written under the boat rule in the paper log, and paper doesn't drown."

"Twenty," Wren said.

"Learn the tower while you're out there," Bayo said. "There's a bell in it. Dead bell. Brass horn on the ninth-floor landing where some fire crew bolted it a hundred years ago, dry cell in a brass box, and it doesn't send. It has no send. All it does is hear."

"Hears what?"

"Last voice. One. Whatever went in last is what's in there and there's no room for two. You talk in that stairwell, she's gone and you're in."

"What makes it play?"

"Still water. Cork on a wire in the horn's throat — water moving lifts the cork, contact opens, she's dumb. Water still lets it shut. Plays once and forgets. Cone's rotted to lace, so it comes out sounding like a man talking through a comb."

"And the water in there?"

"Doesn't move. Stairwell's sealed. Sea came in through the lobby a lifetime ago and stopped in it. Nothing's stirred since. She's sat on one voice as long as that cell's held, and it's held."

"You know a lot about a bell you heard once," Salas said.

"I've been down that stair."

"When?"

"Once."

"You've been down it once and you're still charging my boat a berth."

"I'm charging the boat," Bayo said. "You're riding on it."

Thirty-one on the gauge. The cold came through the neoprene at the small of her back, and then it stopped being cold and went quiet, which was worse.

"Three minutes on Dey," Nia said. "Dark hull's at seventy and closing. Captain says horn at a hundred."

"Not yet," Sol said, from a long way up.

Wren put her hand on the cable above her fist and felt the drum's fine shiver in it, six people and one boat and a barge running with nothing lit, all of it hanging on Bayo's right palm.

Then the pair crackled, and somebody cleared their throat.

Unhurried. Close. Wet. A cough filed down to a scrape, and then nothing.

Bayo's thumb was off the bar. She could hear the rain hitting the deck plate eleven meters over her head.

"That's not me," he said.

"It's not the can either. The can's at forty-two and the can pings."

"The can hasn't got a throat," Bayo said.

Salas was looking at the door, not at her. The lamp on his helmet put a white oval on the frame, and inside the oval there was a landing with a hand's depth of standing water over the treads, and the water did not move at all.

"Forty-two," Wren said, because somebody had to say it and the number was the only thing left in her head that she was sure of.

"You came down this stair last night," Salas said. "No boat. Nobody on the drum. The Marrow was lashed at the Kettle with her deck light off and I could see her from the slot in this door. You came down past me in the dark with your can in your fist."

"I don't have last night."

"I know. I asked you who had my can and you looked at me like I was weather." He moved the lamp off the frame. "You put it on the shelf inside. Then you shut the door on it. Then you went back up the stair without it, and you'd left me fourteen months in here with no line and no light, and I watched you go."

"Salas—"

"You talked to me through the door before you went. I couldn't hear the words. Metal and water. I knew it was you."

Wren reached for the rail to steady herself and got the wall instead, and the wall was furred with something soft that gave under her glove. She went after the last thing Sol had said to her topside, at the rail, in the rain, and found the place where it should have been as smooth as a scooped apple. No fog on it. No sense of having lost anything. That was the part nobody warned you about: it didn't hurt, it just wasn't there, the way a tooth isn't there.

"It's gone," she said. "Whatever Sol told me at the rail. It's gone and I can't even be angry about it."

"Then say things out loud from here on. Somebody up the line writes them down. Paper doesn't drown." He said it the way a man says a thing he has had fourteen months to arrange.

The stairwell was sealed. The sea had come in through the lobby sometime back when the towers were still full of people, and it had lain down in that stair and never got up again. Bolted to the ninth-floor bracket over the landing was a brass horn gone the green of an old coin, its cone rotted to lace so her lamp came through it in spots. Under the throat, on a wire, a cork, resting against two contacts. Nothing down here pushed it.

She opened her mouth. That was the reflex and she hated herself for it, the diver's reflex, you say your name into the dark and wait to see who answers.

Salas got her wrist. He didn't shake his head. He didn't need to. *Whatever goes in last is what's in there, and there's no room for two.*

She shut her teeth on it and felt her pulse in the bite.

Out past the frame the water was moving, the drum's fine shiver coming down the cable, and that was enough to lift the cork off its contacts. The horn stayed dumb.

Then she came level with the door, and the eddy off the tower's flank died, and the cork settled.

It came out of the lace cone thin and dragged, a man talking through a comb, and it said one word.

*Wren.*

Hers. Not a copy of hers. The little upward lift she put on it at the top of every dive so the file would come out of the slate named right, the thing she had never once heard from the outside.

Then the cable shivered again, the cork lifted, and the horn shut for the rest of the world's history.

The shelf was inside the door, in the dark, at the height of her chest. She could not remember putting anything on it.

On Salas's hip the pony bottle's gauge had a red pin at the bottom of the dial, and the pin was standing up.

The red pin was the reserve mark, the line at the bottom of the dial where a bottle stops having gas and starts having pressure. Below it the gauge still gives you a number. The number just isn't yours anymore.

"Ninety seconds," Salas said. "Call it ninety."

"A hundred and three. That was the deck figure and I'm not revising it down at forty-two meters out of manners."

"Then a hundred and three for one man." He turned the bottle so the dial faced her, which was a courtesy, since she could read it fine. "One of us breathes and one of us hangs on the cable."

"We share it. Hundred and three two ways is fifty-one apiece. The drum wants eighty-four to lift us."

"So we come off the bottle at fifty-one with thirty-three seconds of cable still under us."

"Yes."

"Thirty-three seconds is a long time to be wrong."

"It's twenty seconds longer than this conversation."

Bayo's voice came down the pair, thin and flat, the copper doing what copper does to a man's voice. "Drum's got one pull. I said it with my hand on the lever and I'll say it again with my hand on the lever. One."

"One pull," Wren said. "Copy."

The beacon came through the door plate. Not sound exactly; she felt it in her back teeth, one tick every five seconds, patient as a tap with a bad washer. Six hours of battery in it and the can sitting on a shelf eleven centimeters from her hand, waiting to be picked up by somebody who had put it there.

In her thigh pocket she had the field head, a playback head the size of a deck of cards with a thumb crank on the side, the thing she used topside to check a record without cracking the can. She got it out and held it where Salas could see it.

"Wire's one pass," she said. "You drag it over the head and the head wipes it behind itself. That's not a fault. Insurance men wanted it built that way, so a diver's record couldn't be read twice and sold twice."

"You want to crank it now."

"I want to hear what I said to you."

"You'd hear it. Thirty seconds, standing right here, my voice in your ear saying help is coming." He didn't move the lamp. "Then Bayo leans on the lever, and the Line takes the last hour off you on the way up, and you arrive on that deck holding a blank spool and nothing behind your eyes. You'll have spent it. That's the whole of it. You read it down here, you read it for nobody."

She looked at the field head. Her thumb was already on the crank, and had been for some time.

"Up top, then. Deck light, dry feet, and whatever's left in my head above the Line."

"That's the only place a read is worth anything."

"*I told you,*" she said.

"I've been saving it fourteen months," Salas said. "It's better spent on the shelf."

She put the field head away and zipped the thigh pocket, and then she ran a spare carabiner through the empty D-ring on her harness and clipped the gate shut, so the clip was open and waiting and wouldn't swing into her hip on the way up. Her hands did that without her. Two years of doing it in the dark had left her a pair of hands that knew the job better than she did.

"Nia to the drum." The wire again, flat as a ruler. "Two minutes on Dey. Dark hull's at fifty. Captain says horn at a hundred, and she's said it twice, and she wrote it herself so it counts."

"Say the rest," Wren said.

"It's said."

The release on the pocket door was a T-handle on a spindle, and three turns of it backed four steel dogs out of their keepers. Five atmospheres on the far side and five on this one, so the door would swing on nothing, no inrush, no fight. Fourteen months of somebody's air in there, gone stale as a shut room, and a shelf, and her can.

She put her hand on the handle.

"One pull of air," Salas said. "One pull of winch."

"No margin on either."

"None."

"Log it," Wren said, and turned the handle.
